Right angles keep adjacent sides perpendicular, while opposite sides remain parallel and equal.

Assuming every rectangle must have unequal sides.

A square is a special rectangle with all sides equal.

Formula or rule

p% of N = (p/100)N.

Using 100 as a common base makes different quantities easy to compare.

Right angles keep adjacent sides perpendicular, while opposite sides remain parallel and equal.

The dividing point is closer to the endpoint with the larger weight on the opposite coordinate, so the coordinates are weighted averages.

Common mistake

The weight attached to one endpoint uses the opposite ratio part in the coordinate formula.

Formula or rule

Every boundary point has the same radius, so the shape does not stretch longer in one direction.

A circle is equally wide in every direction; an oval is not.

detailedExplanation:
Basic idea

The section formula finds the coordinates of a point that divides a line segment in a given ratio.

How to recognise it

  • Name the two endpoints.
  • Write the ratio m:n in the correct order.
  • Use weighted averages for x-coordinates and y-coordinates separately.

Formula or rule

Internal division: P((mx? + nx?)/(m+n), (my? + ny?)/(m+n)).

Why it works

The dividing point is closer to the endpoint with the larger weight on the opposite coordinate, so the coordinates are weighted averages.

Common mistake

Swapping m and n without checking which endpoint they belong to.

The weight attached to one endpoint uses the opposite ratio part in the coordinate formula.

Class 11 / Statistics and Probability / Statistics

Range

This statistics idea summarises or compares data so patterns become easier to see.

In this lesson you will recognise it, use one clear example, and avoid the common mistake.
detailedExplanation:
Basic idea

This statistics idea summarises or compares data so patterns become easier to see.

How to recognise it

  • List the data clearly.
  • Choose the correct summary measure.
  • Interpret the answer in the original context.

Formula or rule

Mean = sum of values / number of values.

Why it works

A summary number is useful only when it preserves the feature we want to compare, such as centre, spread, or frequency.

Common mistake

Reporting a number without saying what it means.

Always interpret the statistic in context.
realtimeExamples:
Worked classroom example

For data 2, 3, 7, the mean is (2+3+7)/3 = 4.

Class 12 / Calculus / Continuity and Differentiability

Inverse trig derivatives

A derivative measures instantaneous rate of change.

In this lesson you will recognise it, use one clear example, and avoid the common mistake.
detailedExplanation:
Basic idea

A derivative measures instantaneous rate of change.

How to recognise it

  • Identify the function.
  • Apply the derivative rule.
  • Interpret the result as slope or rate.

Formula or rule

d/dx(x?)=nx???.

Why it works

The derivative comes from the limiting value of average rates over smaller and smaller intervals.

Common mistake

Thinking derivative always gives a number.

A derivative can be a function; evaluate it at a point when needed.
realtimeExamples:
Worked classroom example

If f(x)=x?, then f?(x)=2x, so the slope at x=3 is 6.

Where we use it

  • Speed from position
  • Slope of tangent
  • Optimisation

Section formula

The section formula finds the coordinates of a point that divides a line segment in a given ratio.

In this lesson you will recognise it, use one clear example, and avoid the common mistake.
detailedExplanation:
Basic idea

The section formula finds the coordinates of a point that divides a line segment in a given ratio.

How to recognise it

  • Name the two endpoints.
  • Write the ratio m:n in the correct order.
  • Use weighted averages for x-coordinates and y-coordinates separately.

Formula or rule

Internal division: P((mx? + nx?)/(m+n), (my? + ny?)/(m+n)).

Why it works

The dividing point is closer to the endpoint with the larger weight on the opposite coordinate, so the coordinates are weighted averages.

Common mistake

Swapping m and n without checking which endpoint they belong to.

The weight attached to one endpoint uses the opposite ratio part in the coordinate formula.
realtimeExamples:
Worked classroom example

The point dividing A(1,2) and B(4,8) in ratio 1:2 is ((1?4 + 2?1)/3, (1?8 + 2?2)/3) = (2,4).

Where we use it

  • Map locations between two places
  • Dividing a line segment in coordinate geometry
  • Vector position calculations

detailedExplanation:
Basic idea

Probability measures how likely an event is, from 0 to 1.

How to recognise it

  • List possible outcomes.
  • Count favourable outcomes.
  • Divide favourable outcomes by total equally likely outcomes.

Formula or rule

P(event)=favourable outcomes/total outcomes.

Why it works

The ratio compares the event we want with all possible equally likely outcomes.

Common mistake

Counting outcomes that are not equally likely as if they were.

Check whether the outcomes have equal chances first.
